38 What is the rest mass of a beta-particle?
A
0
B
9.11  10–31
kg
C
1.66  10–27
kg
D
1.67  10–27
kg

hints: Recall what particle a beta-particle actually is in beta-minus decay - which lepton is emitted from the nucleus?
Compare the mass scales: an electron mass is about $10^{-30} \text{ kg}$ while a nucleon mass and $1u$ are about $10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Check which listed value in $\text{kg}$ matches the known electron rest mass and which values match a proton or one atomic mass unit.
walkthrough: Identify the particle: a beta-minus particle is an electron emitted at high speed during beta decay, so its rest mass is the electron rest mass.
Recall the rule: photons have zero rest mass, electrons have $m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, while protons, neutrons and $1u$ are near $1.66$ to $1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Compare the options: $0$ would mean massless like gamma radiation, and the two $10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ values are about 2000 times too large for an electron.
Select the value that equals the electron rest mass with correct unit $\text{kg}$.

A.explanation: Zero rest mass is the property of a gamma-photon, not a beta-particle which has non-zero mass.

B.explanation: A beta-particle is a fast-moving electron with electron rest mass of $9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$.

C.explanation: This is $1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, the atomic mass unit $u$, about 1800 times heavier than an electron.

D.explanation: This is $1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, approximately the rest mass of a proton or neutron, not an electron.
